extracted.intended_audience: patent drafters, patent attorneys and practitioners preparing patent applications (international/WIPO guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting and structuring patent claims across multiple claim types and jurisdictions, including how to frame product-by-process, parameter, use, medical, composition, biotechnology and computer-implemented claims and how to design claim scope (broad vs narrow).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of purpose/functional language in claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a claim contains wording indicating a purpose (e.g., "for re-melting galvanic layers"), determine whether that wording is to be treated as a mere statement of suitability for an outcome or as a functional/technical feature defining a step of the claimed method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim is directed to a process that comprises physical steps which result in a product, mentioning its purpose often implies mere suitability (the process need only be suitable to produce the intended outcome) and will not necessarily be treated as an actual method step. Conversely, when purpose wording clearly defines a function of the method (i.e., a functional feature concerning the re-melting of galvanic layers), it should be understood as defining one of the steps of the claimed method. This distinction affects anticipation by prior art: prior art disclosing the same method without indicating the particular product outcome may anticipate a claim that later recites that particular product when the purpose is only suitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that define a product in terms of the process of manufacture (e.g., "Product X obtainable by process Y").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Product-by-process claims are allowable in some jurisdictions but the product must still meet patentability requirements (novelty, inventive step). A product is not automatically novel merely because made by a new process; many jurisdictions construe such claims as claims to the product as such and grant absolute protection to the product. The applicant bears the burden of proving that process differences produce a distinct product (e.g., by demonstrating different properties). Jurisdictional differences exist (e.g., EPO considers purpose when determining features of a product obtained by a process; some jurisdictions treat product-by-process as method claims; Japan may find them indefinite and use only in special circumstances). Professional tip: check permissibility and whether product-by-process is the best strategy in each jurisdiction and consider using it as part of a mix of claim formats. Typical use: complex chemical entities (polymers, foods) difficult to define structurally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parameter claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that define products or process-related features by characteristic measurable values or mathematical formulae (e.g., melting point, flexural strength).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use parameter claims when an invention can only be defined by such terms or defining it structurally would unduly restrict scope, provided the parameters can be directly and positively verified without undue experimentation by tests or procedures specified in the description or known to the skilled person. The drafter should specify constructions and provide directions for routine test procedures to determine parameters. EPO allows parameter characterization when necessary and objectively determinable but may scrutinize such claims as they can disguise lack of novelty. Parameter claims are appropriate where, for example, polymorphs can only be distinguished by infrared spectra or X-ray diffraction patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: General use claims (use claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims seeking protection for a particular purpose of using a product (a subtype of process claims), e.g., "the use of substance X as an insecticide."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In some jurisdictions (e.g., EPO for non-medical uses) such a use claim will be treated as equivalent to a process/method claim (e.g., "a process of killing insects using substance X"). Use claims are not universally accepted (the United States does not treat "use" as a statutory class of claim). When drafting, be mindful of how the claim should be interpreted in the target jurisdictions to avoid unintended product-claim or apparatus interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical indication claims (first/second medical uses and claim formats)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to new medical uses of known products (first or subsequent medical indications), and the various permissible claim formats depending on jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Medical-use inventions require careful attention to national laws and practices as permissibility and scope vary. Common formats include: Swiss-type claims ("use of X in the manufacture of a medicament for the treatment of Y") — historically accepted at EPO (1985–2010) and in many countries; purpose-limited product claims ("substance X for use in the treatment of Y") — compulsory at EPO since 2011 and used in some national laws; plain use claims ("use of X for the treatment of Y") — accepted in some countries (Germany, Canada, Australia); "substance when used to treat" formulations; and method-of-treatment claims ("a method of treating a human having Y comprising administration of X") — accepted in the United States and Australia. Jurisdictional differences extend to patentability, claim format, infringement/enforcement (e.g., U.S. practitioners may be protected from liability and enforcement often focuses on manufacturers/distributors), and whether product claims covering known substances remain patentable when a new medical use is discovered. Professional tip: ensure the first application’s description supports selecting the most appropriate format(s) for jurisdictions of interest and consider including a combination of product, use and process claims (and preparation process claims) to maximize protection and mitigate invalidity risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to the chemical nature, components or formulation of an invention (e.g., electroplating solution compositions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting composition claims, claim each element as narrowly or broadly as necessary relative to prior art and commercial strategy. Specific elements named precisely (e.g., exact compounds and concentrations) are narrower; generic elements (e.g., 'a pH-modifying substrate' sufficient to adjust pH to 3.5–5.0) are broader and capture any compound performing that function. The drafter must balance breadth with clarity and support in the description. Be mindful of jurisdictional special requirements for biotech-related compositions (sequence listings, deposit rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Biotechnology claims and deposit requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims involving biological material where words alone may be insufficient to enable a person skilled in the art (e.g., seeds, microorganisms, DNA sequences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When biological material cannot be fully described in words, access to the material (deposit) may be necessary to satisfy disclosure and statutory requirements. Many jurisdictions require or allow deposit systems; the Budapest Treaty facilitates international recognition of microorganism deposits with International Depositary Authorities (IDAs). Claims can reference deposited samples by accession numbers (example: 'A seed of cotton cultivar designated PHY 78 Acala, wherein a representative sample ... was deposited under ATCC Accession No. PTA-5666'). Ensure compliance with sequence listing and deposit rules in the target jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-implemented invention claims and formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Drafting guidance for inventions involving software, algorithms, data structures, computer-readable media and hardware implementations, considering the exclusion of abstract ideas/software 'as such' in many jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many jurisdictions exclude abstract ideas, software per se, pure mental acts and business methods. Patent applications for computer-implemented inventions typically include product (apparatus/system), method and use claims. The first claim is frequently a method claim because algorithms represent dynamic behavior. Include product claims (e.g., a data-processing system) that refer back to method claims where allowed; where such referencing is not allowed, rephrase method steps as "means for ..." or concrete "a transmitter for sending ..." but note 'means' language (means-plus-function) may be narrowly interpreted in jurisdictions like the U.S. Specialized claim formats include computer-readable medium (Beauregard) claims (preambles like "A computer-readable storage medium storing instructions that when executed by a computer cause the computer to perform a method ...") and data-structure (Lowry) claims (claims to memory/data structures stored in memory). Choose formats with attention to target-jurisdiction practices and evolving case law. Professional tip: stay up to date as practices evolve with technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare the claims first
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin drafting a patent application by preparing the claims before drafting the description and other parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Starting with the claims helps refine the idea of the invention and guides the drafting of the description and other application parts. Claims force the drafter and inventor to clarify the inventive concept and the key elements that should be supported by the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim scope balance: drafting broad and narrow claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft a set of claims that ranges from the broadest to the narrowest to effectively capture the full scope of an invention’s novelty and to provide fallback positions during prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An ideal approach is to draft claims from broadest to narrowest. In practice, it can help to start with a narrow claim of the embodiment then gradually remove or generalize elements to reach the broadest claim. Use abstract/general terms (e.g., 'power source' instead of 'electric motor') where appropriate, but ensure at least one independent claim recites more than one element (in jurisdictions that require it). Keep dependent claims that reintroduce narrowed/omitted features to capture fallback positions. Consider drafting multiple independent claim sets (apparatus, element-focused, method, process) to cover different aspects of the invention; create alternative claim sets only when each truly represents independent novelty of commercial significance or when prior art is unclear. Always check the inventor’s intended commercial scope — if the inventor wants a narrow, specific scope, draft accordingly rather than overbroadly. The drafter should use removed elements as sources for dependent claims (e.g., dependent claims restoring earlier, narrower terms) and may split claim sets to focus on alternative points of novelty.
